content:
When you use an AI headshot generator, your photos are used to train a model on your face and to generate the set you paid for. That part is the same everywhere. What differs between tools, and what you should actually be asking, is whether your photos are used for anything else, how long they are kept, and how you get them deleted.

Below is what any tool does with your photos, the questions worth putting to any provider, what data protection law gives you in general, and then plainly what Picturesk does. No certifications claimed, no vague reassurance, just the actual practice.

What happens to your photos when you use an AI headshot generator?

Three things: training, generation and delivery. Your selfies are used to train a model on your face, that model generates the headshots across the backgrounds and outfits you chose, and the finished set is sent to you. The questions that matter come after that.

Are the photos used to train anything beyond your own set, how long are they stored, can you get them deleted by asking, and who can see them in the meantime? Any honest provider can answer all four in one paragraph.

At a glanceThe fact
What your photos are used forTraining a model on your face and generating your set
Are images of you personal information?Yes: information relating to an identifiable person is personal information (ICO)
Right to have data erasedExists under UK GDPR, but it is not absolute (ICO)
Time a provider has to respond to a requestOne month (ICO)
Photos Picturesk asks for5 to 15 recent selfies, 10 to 12 is the sweet spot
Deletion at PictureskOn request by emailing info@picturesk.ai, not automatic

What does any AI headshot tool actually do with your selfies?

Every serious tool goes through the same three stages, whatever it says on the landing page. First, training: your uploaded photos are used to teach a model what your face looks like from several angles and in several lights. This is why tools ask for more than one photo, and why 10 to 12 varied selfies beats 15 near-identical ones.

Second, generation: the trained model produces new images of you in settings you never stood in, a studio, an office, a brick wall. Third, delivery: the finished files are stored somewhere so they can be sent to you and, usually, so you can download them again later.

Each stage leaves a copy of something. The original uploads, the trained model, and the outputs can all sit on a server after you have closed the tab. That is not sinister on its own, but it is the reason the questions below are worth asking before you upload, not after.

What questions should you ask any provider before uploading?

You do not need to read a whole privacy policy to get the answers that matter. Put these to the provider directly, or search their privacy policy equivalent for them. If the answers are missing or evasive, that is an answer too.

  • Are my photos used to train anything beyond my own set? The key distinction is between a model trained on your face for you, and a general model improved using your face for everyone. You want the first and a clear no on the second.
  • How long are my uploads, the trained model and the outputs kept? A specific answer is better than a reassuring one. "Until you ask us to delete them" is a real answer. "We take privacy seriously" is not.
  • How do I get everything deleted, and how long does it take? There should be a named route, an email address or a button, and a response time you can hold them to.
  • Who can see my photos in the meantime? Staff, contractors, third-party processors. Ask whether humans look at uploads and why.
  • Are my results used as marketing examples? Some tools show customer outputs on their site. You should have to opt in, not opt out.
  • What happens if the generation fails? Not strictly a privacy question, but a provider that refunds automatically on failure tends to have the rest of its process in order as well.

One more practical point: check whether the tool looks at your photos before you pay. A provider that screens uploads for a clear, uncovered face before charging you is showing you its process rather than hiding it.

What does data protection law give you?

More than most people assume, and less than the phrase "right to be forgotten" suggests.

Start with the basic definition. The UK Information Commissioner's Office explains that personal information relates to an identified or identifiable person, and that processing means taking any action with someone's personal information, even where it is deleted quickly. A photo of your face plainly identifies you, so a set of your selfies is personal information in the ordinary sense, and uploading them is processing.

Next, erasure: under UK GDPR, individuals have a right to have personal data erased, also known as the right to be forgotten. The same ICO guidance is clear that the right is not absolute and only applies in certain circumstances, and that an organisation has one month to respond to a request. So you can ask, the provider has to reply within a month, and in the common case of a consumer service holding your photos because you uploaded them, there is rarely a good reason to refuse.

The exact rules depend on where you and the provider are, and this is not legal advice. But the shape is similar across most modern data protection regimes: images of you are personal data, you have a route to ask for deletion, and the provider has a duty to answer. The ICO's own pages, linked above, are the clearest plain-English source if you want the detail.

Why do the photos matter more than the headshots?

Because the uploads are the raw material and the trained model is the reusable part. The finished headshots are images you have already chosen to show the world on LinkedIn or a CV. Your original selfies, taken in your kitchen with no thought given to them, are different: several angles of your face, in one place, tied to your name and payment details.

There is also a research point here that cuts the other way.

A study in Cognition found that different photos of the same unfamiliar face vary so much that people often sort them as different people. That is why a headshot tool needs several photos rather than one to learn what you actually look like. It is also why the bundle of uploads, taken together, is a more complete record of your face than any single photo you have posted publicly.

None of this means you should not use an AI tool. It means the uploads are the thing worth protecting, and the right to ask for their deletion is the thing worth knowing you have.

What does Picturesk do with your photos?

Plainly: we use your photos to train a model on your face and to generate your set, and nothing else. You upload 5 to 15 recent selfies, choose your backgrounds and outfits, pay once, and we train a model on your face, generate the set across the options you chose, and email it in about an hour. That is the whole use.

Before payment, every photo is screened: one clear face, large enough in frame, nothing covering the eyes, and unsafe content rejected. You are told which photos fail and can swap them, so you never pay for input we already know will not work. This is a quality check on the inputs, done before your card is charged.

On retention, the honest answer is that your photos are deleted on request, not automatically. Email info@picturesk.ai and we delete them.

We do not claim a certification, we do not quote a retention period we cannot stand behind, and we do not tell you the files vanish on their own, because they do not. If that matters to you, and it should, send the email once your set has arrived and you are happy with it.

The full detail is on the Picturesk privacy policy. If you want to see the process before uploading anything, the AI headshot generator page walks through the plan, background and outfit choices first, and the photo upload comes after.

Should you wait until your set arrives before asking for deletion?

Yes, and here is why: two refund promises depend on the model and the outputs existing. If a generation run fails, the refund is issued automatically. If the results do not look like you, you reply to the delivery email within 3 days and get a full refund, and you keep the images either way.

A sensible order is: upload, receive the set in about an hour, check it looks like you, then email a deletion request if you want one. You lose nothing by asking a week later, and you keep the guarantee intact in the meantime.

If you are uncertain about any of this, ask before you upload. The contact page is the place, and a straight question deserves a straight answer, from us or from any tool you are considering.

faqs.question: Are my selfies used to train an AI for other people?
faqs.answer: Ask the provider directly, because practice varies. The distinction is between a model trained on your face to produce your set, and a general model improved using your face for everyone. Picturesk uses your photos only to train a model on your face and generate your own set.

faqs.question: Does an AI headshot generator delete my photos automatically?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, and you should never assume it: some tools set a retention period, others keep files until asked. Picturesk deletes photos on request, not automatically: email info@picturesk.ai and they are removed. Check the privacy policy of any tool before uploading.

faqs.question: Are photos of my face personal data?
faqs.answer: Yes. The ICO explains that personal information is anything relating to an identified or identifiable person, and a clear photo of your face identifies you. That means uploading selfies is processing of personal data, and data protection rights such as the right to erasure apply to it.

faqs.question: How long does a company have to delete my photos after I ask?
faqs.answer: Under UK GDPR, an organisation has one month to respond to an erasure request, according to the ICO. The right is not absolute and applies only in certain circumstances, but for a consumer service holding your uploaded selfies there is rarely a good reason to refuse.

faqs.question: Does Picturesk look at my photos before I pay?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every photo is screened at upload, before payment: one clear face, large enough in frame, nothing covering the eyes, and unsafe content is rejected. You are told which photos fail and can swap them, so you never pay for input already known to fail.
